books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: South Carolina, Declaration of the Immediate Causes of Secession (December 24, 1860)
Mississippi, Declaration of the Immediate Causes of Secession (January 9, 1861)
James Buchanan, Fourth Annual Message to Congress (December 3, 1860)

source: original; documents are public-domain primary sources and real data (see each document's sourcing note)
prompt: Evaluate the extent to which the election of 1860 and the secession crisis made the Civil War unavoidable in the period 1860–1861.

documents.title: South Carolina: the compact is broken
documents.source: South Carolina, Declaration of the Immediate Causes Which Induce and Justify the Secession of South Carolina from the Federal Union, December 24, 1860. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: South Carolina's convention, explaining to the world why the state left the Union — a legal case for secession, written after the ordinance of December 20, 1860.
documents.text: . . . We assert that fourteen of the States have deliberately refused for years past to fulfil their constitutional obligations, and we refer to their own Statutes for the proof. . . . Thus the constitutional compact has been deliberately broken and disregarded by the non-slaveholding States, and the consequence follows that South Carolina is released from her obligation. . . . A geographical line has been drawn across the Union, and all the States north of that line have united in the election of a man to the high office of President of the United States whose opinions and purposes are hostile to Slavery.

documents.title: Mississippi: slavery is the cause
documents.source: Mississippi, A Declaration of the Immediate Causes Which Induce and Justify the Secession of the State of Mississippi from the Federal Union, January 9, 1861. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Mississippi's convention, naming slavery as the state's whole position — the frankest of the secession declarations.
documents.text: . . . Our position is thoroughly identified with the institution of slavery—the greatest material interest of the world. Its labor supplies the product which constitutes by far the largest and most important portions of the commerce of the earth. . . . That blow has been long aimed at the institution, and was at the point of reaching its consummation. There was no choice left us but submission to the mandates of abolition, or a dissolution of the Union, whose principles had been subverted to work out our ruin.

documents.title: Crittenden: a line to save the Union
documents.source: Senator John J. Crittenden, proposed amendments to the Constitution (S. No. 50), Article 1, introduced December 18, 1860. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Senator John J. Crittenden of Kentucky, proposing constitutional amendments to settle the crisis — the last major compromise effort.
documents.text: . . . In all the territory of the United States now held, or hereafter acquired, situate north of 36 degrees 30 minutes, slavery or involuntary servitude, except as a punishment for crime, is prohibited while such territory shall remain under territorial government. In all the territory south of said line of latitude, slavery of the African race is hereby recognized as existing, and shall not be interfered with by Congress, but shall be protected as property by all the departments of the territorial government during its continuance.

documents.title: Corwin: slavery protected forever
documents.source: Corwin Amendment, proposed amendment to the Constitution, passed by Congress March 2, 1861. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Congress, proposing an amendment that would have barred any future amendment touching slavery in the states — passed two days before Lincoln's inauguration.
documents.text: No amendment shall be made to the Constitution which will authorize or give to Congress the power to abolish or interfere, within any State, with the domestic institutions thereof, including that of persons held to labor or service by the laws of said State.

documents.title: Buchanan: secession is revolution
documents.source: President James Buchanan, Fourth Annual Message to Congress, December 3, 1860. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: President James Buchanan, in his last annual message — denying secession's legality while holding that the government could not coerce a state.
documents.text: . . . In order to justify secession as a constitutional remedy, it must be on the principle that the Federal Government is a mere voluntary association of States, to be dissolved at pleasure by any one of the contracting parties. If this be so, the Confederacy is a rope of sand, to be penetrated and dissolved by the first adverse wave of public opinion in any of the States. . . . secession is neither more nor less than revolution.

documents.title: Davis: consent of the governed
documents.source: Jefferson Davis, Inaugural Address as provisional president of the Confederate States of America, Montgomery, Alabama, February 18, 1861. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Jefferson Davis, inaugurated as provisional president of the Confederacy at Montgomery — claiming the new government rests on the consent of the governed.
documents.text: . . . Our present condition, achieved in a manner unprecedented in the history of nations, illustrates the American idea that governments rest upon the consent of the governed, and that it is the right of the people to alter or abolish governments whenever they become destructive of the ends for which they were established. . . . We have changed the constituent parts, but not the system of our Government. The Constitution formed by our fathers is that of these Confederate States, in their exposition of it, and in the judicial construction it has received, we have a light which reveals its true meaning.

documents.title: The election of 1860, in numbers
documents.source: Returns of the presidential election of November 6, 1860, as published by the Library of Congress (guides.loc.gov/presidential-election-1860) and the American Presidency Project.
documents.sourcing: The returns of the presidential election of November 6, 1860 — the numbers behind the crisis.

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which the election of 1860 and the secession crisis made the Civil War unavoidable, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as the failure of compromise in the 1850s, the Kansas-Nebraska Act, the Dred Scott decision, or the rise of the Republican Party.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument, or background from a later century, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (first point): earns the point for describing specific and relevant evidence from at least three documents to support an argument about the prompt.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than three documents, or quoting documents without describing what they show, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support an argument, with the evidence accurately described and tied to the claim.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or listing documents without connecting them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence beyond the documents: earns the point for describing a specific and relevant example beyond the documents, such as the Democratic split at Charleston and Baltimore, the firing on Fort Sumter, Lincoln's call for 75,000 volunteers, or the secession of the Upper South.
rubric.notEarned: A general statement with no specific example beyond the documents does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining the relevance of a document's author, purpose, audience, or historical situation to the argument, for at least two documents.
rubric.notEarned: Identifying an author without explaining why it matters, or sourcing only one document, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for demonstrating a complex understanding, such as qualifying the extent of the claim, showing how the same development pulled in opposite directions, or weighing change against continuity.
rubric.notEarned: A second example with no qualification or weighing does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: The election of 1860 and the secession crisis made the Civil War unavoidable to a great extent, because the election broke the party system that had managed the slavery question, and every effort to repair it failed on the one point neither side could surrender — slavery in the territories — though war still needed the Fort Sumter crisis to turn a political break into shooting.
Grouping 1 — the election as a sectional verdict: the returns (Doc 7) show Lincoln winning 180 electoral votes with under 40 percent of the popular vote, and South Carolina (Doc 1) reads the result as a Northern line drawn across the Union.
Grouping 2 — slavery as the cause, in the seceders' own words: Mississippi (Doc 2) ties its whole position to slavery, and Davis (Doc 6) claims the consent of the governed for a new government built on the old Constitution.
Grouping 3 — the last efforts fail: Crittenden (Doc 3) offers a permanent line at 36 degrees 30 minutes, and Corwin (Doc 4) offers to shield slavery in the states forever, yet the compromise dies on the territories; Buchanan (Doc 5) calls secession revolution but claims no power to stop it.
Outside evidence: the Democratic split at Charleston and Baltimore, which put two Democrats on the ballot; the firing on Fort Sumter on April 12, 1861, and Lincoln's call for 75,000 volunteers, which brought Virginia, Arkansas, Tennessee, and North Carolina into the Confederacy.
Complexity: the war was unavoidable in the sense that no compromise could hold once the election made the territories the test, yet it was not foreordained in its timing — the Upper South waited five months, and only Sumter and the troop call turned secession into war.
